review_text_raw:
I have a confession.

I like goofy fake hacking scenes in movies.

I know it's not indicative of "actual" hacking, and as a programmer I should probably be a little miffed at how unrealistic they make the whole thing seem. But I don't care! I love it anyway.

Hacknet promised to give me that kind of feeling, and like Uplink before it, it kinda did. It's a puzzle game where your tools are 'hacking programs' and your problems relate to breaking into computers and grabbing info, deleting info, or causing chaos.

It works well, and it reveals just how satisfying it is to solve software problems, even when it's heavily abstracted and simplified.

But my biggest problem with Hacknet is that it never really takes that next step into something greater than a simplified hacking game. Toward the end of the game there's a distinct feeling of "That was it?"

Want to hack an SSH port? Then use SSHportHack.exe. Want to hack an FTP port? Then use FTPportHack.exe. The entire game is like this. For each problem or situation there's almost always exactly one answer, and there are few opportunities to feel clever. 

In some ways the game actually feels unfinished. Many computers you hack into contain generically named folders that are either empty or have snippets of IRC conversations from Bash.org. The game is set in modern times, yet your computer only has ~800mb of RAM and you can never upgrade it. The UI for selecting systems to hack into is an absolute nightmare.

There are even mechanics that don't seem to actually...exist? For example, a big deal is made about deleting your logs and leaving no trace behind - a classic hacking trope - yet I never once saw any consequences for forgetting. I eventually just stopped clearing logs and it never was a problem

As I said, I like Hackers-style hacking. It's fun and goofy and still scratches the same itch as actual hacking. Hacknet gets close, but its far too shallow and misses the mark.

review_text_raw:
I'm not entirely sure what the target demographic is for this game. It's an ostensibly terminal-based game running on a UNIX platform, but it has minimal overlap with bash commands, and trying to treat it like bash will only get you confused. 

So, this must be aimed at people without any tech background. However, how much fun can someone uninterested enough in coding to not care about this have, if all they're doing is typing in the same auto-completing commands over and over into a terminal?

Oh, and you can't scroll on the terminal, too. On the other hand, the GUI is both cluttered and unintuitive. Everything feels horrid to use.

It claims to feature "REAL HACKING", but the hacking consists of running magic hack spells via the terminal, and, if you DO know anything about hacking, that makes a lot of what the game asks of you feel obtuse. It took me so long to realise that I was supposed to open up a shell on my own PC, which, if crashed, would somehow take down a proxy server hosted elsewhere? I was assuming I had to find some kind of initial access mechanism to bypass the proxy and execute shellcode on the target PC, but, uh, I guess crashing the equivalent of cmd.exe on my computer really is the future of hacking.

The story is okay, I guess. At least it was easy to 100%.

My advice to anyone interested in a hacking-type game aimed at beginners is to check out the (free!) OverTheWire Bandit wargame, instead; it's fun, and it'll actually teach you something useful.

The gameplay basically consists of nothing but navigating folders. There's no coding to be done, no puzzles to be solved. 
All you'll do is connect to "computers" (folders), run a program that magically "hacks" your way into them, scan for more "computers" to "hack", rinse and repeat. It is mind numbing and repetitive.

I kept playing because I thought surely something interesting must happen eventually, but I was wrong. The most challenging problem you'll have to solve is writing down a password to use on a locked folder.

If you want to feel like a super smart hacker without having to put in any actual effort, you might like this game. If you were looking for a real puzzle game, then look elsewhere.

review_text_raw:
"Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. This creates a truly immersive experience and puts players right in the thick of trying to break through the firewalls."

Blatant lies. Hacknet is straight up Hollywood hacking. The terminal is a simplistic cross-breed between bash and cmd.exe. It puts you in the role of a script kiddy, who "hacks" systems by observing which ports are open on the target machine and running the corresponding hacking program by typing its name and a port number (e.g. "FTPHack 21"). Once you're in, your job is to either snoop through some files for a password, to download files, or to delete them using basic terminal skills. You're supposed to cover your tracks by deleting logs, but it rarely matters. The same thing, over and over, no brains required. There's no sense you're accomplishing anything of value, nor of any consequence to yourself or others.

It's an insult to anyone with more than a surface-level understanding of network security, as challenging to a puzzle gamer as 50 consecutive games of Tic-tac-toe, and isn't even that interesting in terms of Hollywood hacking simulations. It's on par with a budding game developer's first project, not something worth spending $10 to $24 on. If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100).

That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.

Final Update (3):
Seeing as the dev doesn't seem to give a damn anymore about providing the patches necessary to have the game work as advertised in a timely manner, I won't check on it or update the review any further.
Maybe the game will someday be what it should've been from day 1, but 3 weeks early access quality for a full release isn't acceptable.

-------------------------------------------------------------

Sadly, this has to be a [b]not recommended[/b] review.
The reason for this is the apparent lack of quality control before release. See details below.

First off, the concept is great. I really want to love this game for it's concept. It is basically a much better version of Uplink.
Now, is it realistic from a hacking point of view? No. But that's a good thing, because realistic hacking scenarios would be pretty boring for a game. The concepts are taken from the real world and simplified/modified to make an interesting game.

It is simple at first and doesn't get too difficult while still providing some challenges and a nice storyline. 

That being said, while the game could be a 9/10, game-breaking bugs currently make it at most a 4/10.

Here are some that I've encountered so far:
- You are able to take multiple contracts at some point, but doing so will prevent further progression due to the quest completion system being bugged.
- Using multiple profiles is inconsistent, you can't be sure that your savegame remains the way it was
- Game supports windowed mode but crashes regularly if you focus on another window
- Loss of all savegames - this is a big one. The last time the aforementioned crash occured, I've lost all of my saves.

The last bug on this list is the main reason this review has come to a not recommended conclusion and the others severely contributed.
If any beta testing would've been done, such a list of game-breaking bugs wouldn't exist.

Update 1: After the most recent patch promised a solution  to "many issues that were causing people to lose save files" I've decided to start a new profile. Did some work, saved session and exited the game normally. And alas, as I started the game again today there were no accounts and my save_accountsMeta.xml was gone. Again. This is clearly getting ridiculous and I wouldn't expect a solution any time soon, the dev will probably need a few weeks to figure out the issues with Steam API/Cloud saves etc.

Update 2: Since apparently fixing the savegame issues within a reasonable amount of time isn't happening, I have to say this is close to false advertising. The game should be tagged early access if the amount of issues is still that extensive after two patches. This is the sort of behaviour I'd expect from large companies that simply don't give a sh*t anymore, not form an indie dev trying to make his name. I hope the dev learns some things from this failed release, one of them being that you shouldn't release a game full of bugs when you're too busy being at conventions after the release and don't have time to fix the issues.

Don't get me wrong: everyone makes mistakes and stuff like that can happen. But that doesn't change the fact that as a customer I kinda feel cheated, since there's a reason I don't buy early access and this time the product isn't of higher quality.
Again, once the major bugs are fixed and solutions for the existing issues are presented, I'll gladly give this game a recommendation.

review_text_raw:
I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

PREFACE: I only played this game for one hour, and this may be a biased review, but so far I didn't see anything worth pursuing. The game may get interesting further down, but it just didn't pique my interesting so far.

This game does way too much hand holding to be enjoyable. If you're a casual gamer who wants to get the feeling that you're a cool hacker, go for it, but if you want any actual challenge, this game is not for you.

The whole game is just reading long emails trying to get the important information, then running the same sequence of commands over and over for every challenge. Every time they want to make it harder, they just add one more command to this sequence and repeat the same process.

There was very little problem solving or experimenting happening, which to me is what hacking is all about. Trying things out yourself and learning new tools. Not someone telling you what to do each step of the way.

The terminal interface was neat and the soundtrack was banging, but the game was just too bland and repetitive to be enjoyable.

review_text_raw:
[+] Soundtrack
[+] User Interface

[-] Plot
[-] World design and interaction

I bought this game mainly for its soundtrack, then because I'm a terminal guy myself and I love typing commands.
From this standpoint the game is beautiful: hastily keyboard mashing while listening to Gallego's killer tracks was awesome, not even mentioning the time when Carpenter Brut took over...

This game perfectly sets the mood for an awesome experience, with its music, its terminals and pseudo-graphical GUIs... but then falls short story-side.

[b]The plot is dull, linear and somewhat predictable.[/b]
You only have one bifurcation of the storyline that's even non-obvious to unlock. It gives you access to some more interesting missions, a new faction, and let you see a dark corner of the in-game Internet; but then it merges back into the main path in an abrupt way, as meaningless as it could get.
Yes, there are some interesting easter eggs and strange computer systems, but nothing that makes you want to explore on your own all that much.
There's only, like, [i]one[/i] moral choice, and it's not even part of the main quest.

[b]Whatever you do, whoever you damage, there's no consequence. The world simply doesn't react.[/b]
No cops backtracing you, no factions you can anger, no reputation system: you're part of the Good Guys from start to finish; you can screw up all the machines you want, you are The Savior and no one will change that.
Heck, you can even fail hacks and, apart from a panicking minigame to atone, no officer nor corporate killer will ever knock on your door.
You're simply bounced from a Good faction to another, without any chance to express your will. Just keep on hacking. Don't even bother to cover up your footprints. Logs are useless.

In the end, yes you can buy it, sure, but don't expect much except aesthetics.


[TECHNICAL NOTE]
The in-game console is backed by your native OS, and everything is deeply woven with its runtime.
Yes, you read it right.
That means two things:
[list]
    [*] if some of your game files break, you can be welcomed by an OS error printed on the console;
    [*] while this game runs on both Windows and Linux and has cloud sync, the save files are [b]not[/b] cross-platform; I suspect it has to do with different text encodings (save files are simple XMLs), and you need a repair tool you can find on the forums in order to convert them.
[/list]
Yeah, that wasn't nice.

I very rarely review games on Steam, and only review the ones about which I am most passionately moved, positively or negatively.  In this case, negatively.  In contrast to my usual, I have enabled comments on this review -- feel free to state your feedback, whether you agree with me or not, just please remain respectful to me, the developers, other commenters, and anyone else as applicable.

There's a "TL;DR" at the end if you're lazy.

I'll start positive.  This game is crazy fun.  It is probably the funnest hacking-themed game I've ever played, and I've played a lot of them.  It was fun and helpful to see some things I recognize from real life, such as the default system port numbers being accurate and the existence of a few UNIX commands (my main OS has been FreeBSD for years, and my experience with UNIX helped with the gameplay in a way that felt good).  I liked seeing the C# source code and realizing it was actual, real C# source code that would probably work if the LESS_THAN was properly changed to a "<" sign, etc (C# is my main dev language, always a plus to see it referenced in a game at all).  That was cool, and I'll probably compile it later to have that tool on my PC for real (don't comment about the related real life security to this -- I assure you I already know, and it's just for fun).  The pacing was really good, and I got hooked fast.  So fast that I immediately bought the DLC, soundtrack, and DLC soundtrack for myself, then bought the game and DLC for both my wife and her boyfriend also.  Despite my negative review, I don't regret this decision at all, it's a very, very fun game.  Oh, the event thing that I can't discuss without giving spoilers, but well, the one where you need to get that thing back, that was super fun!  (Unimportant to the review and a spoiler:) I instinctively [spoiler]jumped to my host and forkbombed, apparently I was supposed to kill his forkbomb instead, oh well... I had already made a backup of that file just in case[/spoiler].  But anyway, the game was extremely fun, looks great, the music is great, and I'm excited to keep playing and see where things take me.

But there are two issues which were severe enough that they prompted me to leave a negative review despite all this.

The first issue isn't so bad and is easily rectified: This game is the pinnacle of Hollywood-style hacking.  It does it very well, and it references real hacking concepts in the game's flavor text and other areas.  Some tools are named the same as real ones, and you will probably learn a few real UNIX system port numbers, but that's about where the realism ends.  Oh, and [b]this wouldn't bother me in the slightest[/b] -- I love Hollywood-style hacking sim games! -- but it clearly says this in the "Features" section in the game's Steam page description, which to me is [u]blatant false advertisement[/u]:

[quote]
Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it.
[/quote]

If I stated what I consider my qualifications for knowing what constitutes "Hollywood-style" hacking, nobody would believe me, so I won't.  But even if you have never seen either a vtty or Hackers, I feel like anyone looking at the animation for the command called "porthack", god and the command name itself, and how it works, and everything related to the actual process of hacking (kinda the core concept in the entire game)... well I just think it doesn't take an expert to realize it's about as unrealistic as you can get.  If you don't believe me and this matters to you, buy the game and try it.  You will know I'm right within the 2 hour window to return it for a full refund, I assure you.  There is no "SSHCrack", no "FTPBounce", these wouldn't be PE executables if they did exist, PE doesn't even run on UNIX, "opening ports" and having requirements for a certain arbitrary number of open ports to "porthack" is very Hollywood.  Stahp.  Hollywood-style hacking is fine, don't be ashamed of it!  But most importantly, [b]advertise this game for it's many strengths, not for a falsehood[/b].  This game doesn't need lies to make it sound good, it's already a good game.  It's already a [i]great[/i] game.  Don't make false claims that sour its image.

Ok, now for the big one (to me).  Some people, many perhaps, won't care about this but I care.  I am quite literally sick to my stomach right now.  This has perhaps very minor spoilers for a very small number of optional (so far where I am in the story) missions, so I will spoiler-tag a lot to be safe, but even if you haven't played the game and hate spoilers, you probably won't be upset for reading the spoiler-tagged text in the next paragraph, it's the mildest of mild spoilers.

So, some of the missions require you to access a database of [spoiler]death row records[/spoiler] and modify them.  The missions are fine, and the topics are relevant.  I thought this was a positive thing to include in the game... until I gained access to this database and actually started reading the records.  I read about 40 of them in a row, unable to stop.  These were not made up, they were real records.  They had to be.  Surely the names were changed at least, right?  I Googled one at random and sure enough it was entirely real, and even the name, age, and date matched.  The [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] were their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler], verbatim.  There is literally a massive database of actual real people's [spoiler]deaths[/spoiler] including their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] in the game, and there are missions to modify this database!  It is making light of a very serious topic with real people's real, actual names, turning it into a game.  If I am [spoiler]executed[/spoiler], I don't want my [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] to be made into a fun, "cool" game.  That's awful!  These families are mourning!  Please do not take real, actual tragedy and juxtapose it alongside comical IRC chat logs!  In a game?!  If you are a U.S. company, the families of these people may have legal justification to press charges.  I almost hope they do.  But instead of that, I would rather you modify your game and replace the real data with artificial data that you make up, or at least change the names and please also [spoiler]their last words[/spoiler].  This would have been such a cool set of missions, with a positive political message, but since you used real data it ruins the whole thing and instead makes it a mishandled slog of insensitivity... or... words, I just hate that you used real data for this.  Please replace it with artificial data.  It won't hurt the game.  It will take a single developer a day, if that, and then you can be on the right side of things, morally and honestly probably legally.  I plan to ask my lawyer his opinion on this sometime when he's not busy, not to press charges myself (I'm not listed in the data), but just out of legal curiosity if charges could be pressed for something like this.

Anyway this is a fun game and I'm not going to try to refund it, I'm not even going to stop playing it, but I will stop recommending it or buying it for more people (I have a tendency to buy games I like repeatedly for lots and lots of people, friends, family, etc.).  I think I bought Necesse 12 or 13 times?  I also fully plan to modify this review if my issues are addressed.  I will do so as soon as I notice the changes.  If you reply to this review when you've addressed them, I will likely notice faster and therefore update it faster... you know, if you don't want one nerd girl's negative review.

TL;DR: Great game, super fun.  But it uses false advertising on its Steam page, and is horribly insensitive to real mourning families IRL, and doesn't even change the names.

-- Amy

review_text_raw:
This game is... mediocre. The gameplay is monotonous and unchallenging, the storyline is fractured and uninspiring (it's even harder to take seriously since you're playing as a script kiddie), and the material is extremely far from reality.  As an actual Linux sysadmin, I am in particular annoyed by how poorly implemented common UNIX utilities are.  "ls *" and "rm ./*" fail, but "rm *" works? No "cp" or "mkdir"?  No way to delete directories? I can go on and on. Literally, I programmed more coreutils in a single college project than there are in this game. Couldn't they have just used busybox or something?  It certainly would have solved the issues the game has with file duplication in directories, since it'd be using actual files, rather than what is presumably a stack/queue/list/whatever.  And I would kill for io redirection.
Also, I'm mildly triggered by the executables being .exe files, but I'm definitely amused that you BSOD instead of kernel panicking.
I bought this game for a song, but I don't think I'd even recommend it if it were free, because in the time it takes you to play this game, you could have learned all sorts of actual UNIX commands in an actual terminal emulator on Linux, something that actually is free -- and you'd probably have a lot more fun, too.

BUGS:
- You can wipe the logs on any server without admin access.
- 89.220.121.48:/eos/apps/birds_8 is listed twice.
- Leaving a server and coming back resets the trace timeout without resetting your progress, which means that the trace timeout never actually matters.
- Uploading a file to a path containing another file with the same name, results in two files with the same name.
- The password for the Timekeeper's Vault doesn't actually work.

review_text_raw:
This is an OK game. I wouldn't go as far as to compare it to either Uplink or the Street Hacker series simply because it feels more like a demo when compared to them. The execution and gameplay is shallow and naive. It's plagued by many basic design issues and most of the missions are just boring, repetitive, and feel more like a chore rather than a challenge.

My biggest gripes are:
-boring, repetitive and easy missions. Only 2 interesting missions stand out, the final Bit one, and the online pacemaker one.
-no sense of urgency or challenge. If you get caught hacking, that's just a reload to last checkpoint. No point in deleting any logs the way Uplink makes sure that you do. Uplink kept you on your toes because getting caught meant absolute game over!
-Badly designed UI. The workstation "map" is a cluttered mess especially as you move closer towards the end. Nodes are being randomly generated and the ones closest to the edge of the screen have their hover information cut off. How that ever went past the testers, I do not know!
-Weird writing, bad grammar, spelling mistakes, juvenile jokes scattered here and there. The ending was incredibly cheesy and anti-climactic.

Not a bad game to get on sale. But this is no Uplink for sure. The tagline shouldn't be "if you liked Uplink, you'll love this!" It's more the other way around because now I definitely feel like going back and replaying Uplink for the zillionth time! :)

Really sucks, this game is great when it works.

Great idea - terrible execution. For the whole duration of the game you perform same actions again, again and again. And again. Oh, and AGAIN. The totally optional Clicker mini-game and tutorial are the best and most memorable parts of it, and that's saying something.

All of this game's content can be listed as follows:
do {

*check your email, get contract details*
probe
-- Oh, heck, a proxy again.
connect xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect yyy.yyy.yyy.yyy
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect zzz.zzz.zzz.zzz
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect... -- nah, that's probably enough, I still need to "hack" that firewall.
*overloading proxy*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
*Proxy bypassed*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
solve XXXXXXX
WebServerWorm 80
SMTPoverflow 25
FTPbounce 21
SSHcrack 22
*waiting until the end of it*
porthack
*waiting again*
-- Finally.
*doing same repeatative stuff on the hacked machine, clear logs, disconnect*

} while true;

And that's about it. You don't even have to think. At all. More than that, you actually CAN'T think to improve something in your game. Everything you do here is just following instructions like a machine. Bypass Propxy, solve Firewall, open ports, hack ports, get data, clear logs, disconnect, rinse and repeat. Since I didn't actually finish the game, I guess there will be more "hacking tools" introduced, but it won't change anything. The core of the game stays the same - just mindless repetition. This has nothing to do with actual cybersecurity business.

The moral side of some contracts is also questionable, to say the least. They want you to:
- get a private medical card of a person (for the sake of curiosity of some idiot forum-dweller);
- forge a degree for some "ally guy" of the (illegal) group you're working for.
- bring the secret [strike]KFC[/strike]CFC spice recepie out to the public, just, you know, for fun;
And that's only what I've encountered so far.

Some of the more "officially looking" contracts also make little sense. Like the one given to you by a high school administration, where you need to get IT admin password, so the administration can personally investigate a suspicion of IT department sharing student's emails data with outsiders (presumably, student's parents). It's so ridiculously stupid it could actually be another (one of many) dev's attempt at humour.


A word of advice:
If you suddenly became interested in all this "terminal net graph hacker cool" thing, just get VMWare\Oracle, download some Linux distros and build your own virtual network to play with. Way more fun, inherently legal and educative way of spending hours upon hours of your time typing stuff in CLI.

review_text_raw:
Good: 
[list]
    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server. At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment. I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

review_text_raw:
I'd only recommend this game if: you get it for free or really cheap, you want a short game to play but don't care what, or you just really want to see lots of scrolling lines and feel like a faux hacker

Otherwise, I don't think it's worth your time for the following reasons:

1. too simple and repetitive
Once you figure out the command lines after a few minutes that's the entire game play. In fact, you'll have to type the same things over so many times you'll mostly use the GUI menu instead. Then, you just wait around all the time waiting for the same 4-5 port hacks to finish that's nothing more than progress bars and flashing numbers like you see in movies. You do this again and again over the next few hours doing simple contracts you pick up from the hacker group postings board (which don't require any thinking since they tell you exactly where to go and what to do which is most of the time just deleting some files off the target server). 

2. lack of story and immersion
As mentioned above, 90% of the time you are doing these simple job postings. The other 10% is the actual story but other than a quick introduction to the missing dead hacker in the beginning, all of its related missions are shoehorned at the end in like the last three missions. Also, another problem I had was the immersion. If you read the files in the folders they want you to target, they're related to the back story of the mission you're doing but if you poke around in the home folder they're just a bunch of random files. For example, it doesn't make sense to read irc chat logs of teenagers making dumb pun jokes and a grocery list in an enterprise server.

3. some poor ui choices
Every IP address you visit is pinned on a board as a node that you can revisit at anytime. However, the nodes become very cluttered towards the end of the game, and critical story nodes at the end are overlapped with a bunch of nodes you visited at the start of the game. I got stuck for a bit for one mission because when I scanned for connected networks I could not see the one out of the five that newly showed up which I needed to go to. It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times.

4. feature bypass/abuse
There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.

review_text_raw:
This might just be the 10 years since launch, or my actual experience with computers, but the gameplay loop feels a bit off (pun not intended) for me. The tutorial got me curious enough with the plot to get through, but there is no substance in the base game. Haven't played the DLC, not interested.

If you are into looking at hacker-looking interfaces and typing the same half a dozen commands over and over (tab complete and up key for history available), you will enjoy it. If you want anything that is anymore puzzling than following clear instructions, look elsewhere.

Basically: 1- open an email, 2- click email attachments for a target IP and maybe add a mission summary note to the screen, 3- click a button to connect to said IP and click another button to Probe the system, 4- run the same 2-5 commands on the same list of ports, 5- browse the filesystem to either find or place a file at mostly the same folders, 6- erase all logs and disconnect, 7- repeat. That's it. The game has a simplified terminal emulator missing a few basic features but fine, you can mostly use it to get things done instead of the GUI except when emailing (mostly). There are no puzzles, the exploits are literal executables you run and wait, the only variability is whether the target machine has proxies or a firewall then you gotta login into a bunch of places you already hacked first and run a shell overload (run and wait) then run a firewall analyzer to unscramble a keyword (run and read). Sometimes you gotta disconnect before a tracing timer runs out, which is never an issue until a single mission has like a 3 seconds timer but same difference. If you do *somehow* get traced, you might need to do the one different thing and change your IP address by... following steps 1 through 6! Or just reboot. Yeah, that's it: steps 1-7, sprinkle disconnects according to timer and if something fails just reboot and resume as usual is the whole game. There are two routes if you accept an optional mission but rest assured, same gameplay eveywhere.

review_text_raw:
The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

review_text_raw:
Premise is engaging and the game is cheap, but it certainly is a no-buy for me.

The game loop goes like this:
[olist]
[*] You receive a contract from one of the many contract hubs in the game.
[*] After receiving it, you will have to hack a computer and gain access to it.
[*] Once you have access, you'll have to search through its folders in order to find information and more nearby computers to hack. You might also find some more new tools.
[*] After you are done, you have to delete the logs of your target computer and disconnect.
[*] If you are not done, hack any remaining computers you found on step 3 until you get the objective done.
[*] Get a new contract.
[/olist]

Hacking progress goes like this: remote computers have a different number of closed ports which you have to open with commands that you acquire as you progress. Each open port lowers the toughness of the target computer and, once it's low enough, you can use a magic command to hack it and gain access to its contents. There are a few extra things (proxies, firewalls, time limit and some per-mission modifications) but overall the process is tedious and revolves around repeating the same commands over and over.

Some other reviews mention that this game has some learning potential, which is wrong. The commands that you execute take no arguments and just show progress bars which go up at the same constant rate, forcing you to be glaring at your screen until they are done. Any resemblance to an actual UNIX command is just the fact that they are, indeed, executed on a terminal emulator.

The game got tedious after an hour. If you enjoy the loop, you might enjoy the game, but be advised that it is repetitive, almost non-interactive and a bit dull. The story is not engaging at all and just revolves around people asking you to hack things.

Overall, it's a repetitive, but very visually and aurally satisfying, clicker/visual novel game. The best features are meant for multiplayer. You're warned to wipe logs early in the game, but logs are useless since there isnt anyone to read them (I stopped clearing them about halfway). Many of the features (like "forkbomb" and the trap functionality of the shells) are completely useless without multiplayer. There are no enemy hackers (save one, who is a major story character and only attempts to hack you once). The world is not alive. It is essentially a visual novel treasure hunt, where you go from one node to the next, doing the same things over and over with the incentive to just finish the game. The story and storytelling arent even good enough to justify it being this way. Maybe when it has multiplayer, itll be worth playing. Overall, the feeling of urgency isn't there like it would be if you were playing a game like slavehack.

When it gets multiplayer, if the multiplayer works correctly, it could well be one of the funnest and most exciting hacking games ever. Until then, unless you think the idea of writing commands instead of doing the same exact thing with a mouse is a good experience, I would probably just get uplink.

Also, if you're reading this review devs, Duckman should be expanded on. He's easily the best character in the game. Thanks Duckfam, you unsung hero.

It is difficult to make a game that captures the feel of hacking. A hacker is successful because he has a large body of knowledge to pull from. He tries a thousand different things before something works.

Making an exciting game about hacking is like making an exciting game about coming up with new mathematical theorems. 

Hacknet is far more fun that I expected, but that isn't saying much. You are given four or five scripts to run with various levels of time pressure. There is a lot of good flavor, being able to customize your UI, using a simplified UNIX, and accessing system files.

Sadly, the gameplay wasn't enough to keep me playing and the story, while interesting, wasn't original enough to carry the game.

review_text_raw:
I hoped this game would be a spiritual successor to Uplink maybe with a little bit more realism. Unfortunately the game falls short of that aspiration.

First of all, it's not any more realistic than Uplink. While you get to use real Unix commands, you don't use them in a very similar way to the real thing. Have no illusion, this game will not teach you anything useful in real life. There's nothing wrong with making your hacking sim game a little over the top with fancy animations and misused tech lingo, but it's not what I expected.

Where the game really fails to live up to Uplink, however, is depth. Remember how Uplink had news bulletins reporting on your mischief, other active hackers taking assignments and getting arrested when you rat on them, multiple banks with multiple accounts wiring funds to each other, and a stock market where you could watch your victim corporations suffer losses after you hack and destroy their mainframes? You will find nothing like this in Hacknet. All you get it a lot of random IRC logs pasted from bash.org and some personal files and emails that are not written in a breathtaking way.

Is it fun? Yeah, especially if it's your first game of this kind. There's a thrill in accessing systems and files you shouldn't be looking at and there's even an overarching plot that's encouraging you to keep playing, but it all lacks depth, gameplay-wise, story-wise and writing-wise.
